shapes.name: Fact
shapes.definition: A single piece of information to be known, stated without argument.
shapes.recognition: Stand-alone assertions: a date, a name, a figure, a rule of the institution, stated once and not argued.

shapes.name: Concept
shapes.definition: A term with a definition, its critical features and examples.
shapes.recognition: A defined term: "X is", "X refers to", a named idea followed by what it means and instances of it.

shapes.name: Structure
shapes.definition: The parts of a thing and how they fit together, where the arrangement itself carries meaning.
shapes.recognition: An anatomy, template or format: labelled elements, a fixed order of parts, a layout whose positions matter.

examples.note: Sets out the fixed, labelled element order for a books, journal-article and web-page reference, each under its own bolded sub-label.

shapes.name: Classification
shapes.definition: Items that sort into categories by stated criteria.
shapes.recognition: "Types of", "kinds of", "can be grouped into": categories named with their members or the criterion that separates them.

shapes.name: Procedure
shapes.definition: Steps a learner performs, in order, to complete a task.
shapes.recognition: Imperative steps, numbered how-to, sequencing words such as first, then, next and finally, addressed to the learner.

shapes.name: Process
shapes.definition: How something works or unfolds over time, described rather than performed by the learner.
shapes.recognition: Stages, phases or a cycle that happen, often in the third person: how a system, cycle or practice unfolds.

shapes.name: Principle
shapes.definition: A rule, guideline or value, with its reasons, about what should or should not be done.
shapes.recognition: "Should", "always", "avoid", "never", values or standards stated with the reason for them.

examples.note: Names the ICAI's six fundamental values of academic integrity (Honesty, Trust, Fairness, Respect, Responsibility, Courage) with the significance of each.

shapes.name: Contrast
shapes.definition: Two versions of the same thing, one stronger than the other.
shapes.recognition: Weak and strong, before and after, draft and revision, or one approach stated to be better than another.

examples.note: Sets quotation against paraphrase and states that paraphrasing is "clearly far more skilful".

shapes.name: Parallel options
shapes.definition: Alternatives, each valid in its own situation, none better overall.
shapes.recognition: Options tied to contexts: disciplines, genres or purposes, "depending on", with no ranking between them.

examples.note: Lists seven referencing styles (author-date/Harvard, MHRA, Chicago, APA, Vancouver, IEEE, OSCOLA), each tied to the disciplines that use it, with none ranked above another.

shapes.name: Pairs
shapes.definition: Items that belong together one to one.
shapes.recognition: Two forms of the same thing, or items with a partner: a citation and its reference-list entry, a term and its definition, a cause and its effect.

shapes.name: Error
shapes.definition: Something that contains a mistake or an omission to be found.
shapes.recognition: Warnings about common mistakes, inaccuracies or missing elements; "avoid"; flawed examples.

shapes.name: Assembly
shapes.definition: A whole built from given parts in a required form.
shapes.recognition: Formatting rules and templates to fill: "set out as", required elements in required order, to be produced by the learner.

examples.note: Gives the required elements and order for a learner to produce a books, journal-article or web-page reference themselves.

shapes.name: Judgement
shapes.definition: A decision with trade-offs, where reasonable choices differ.
shapes.recognition: "When to", "choose", "decide", dilemmas, options whose worth depends on circumstances and weighing.

shapes.name: Criteria
shapes.definition: Concrete checks to apply to one's own work.
shapes.recognition: Checklists, "before you submit", "make sure", yes-or-no tests of a piece of work.

shapes.name: Reflection
shapes.definition: A prompt for the learner's own thinking, practice or experience.
shapes.recognition: "Consider", "think about", "in your own", questions with no single right answer that address the learner.

examples.note: The task box asks the learner to define each of the six fundamental values first, before reading on, with no single right answer.
